objectives: Describe caldera-forming supereruptions (Yellowstone, Toba) and the VEI 7-8 magnitude range.
Explain the 1815 Tambora eruption and its link to the 1816 'Year Without a Summer'.
Quantify how stratospheric sulfate aerosols force climate through changes in radiative balance.

slides.title: Calderas and supereruptions
slides.body:
The largest explosive eruptions on Earth do not build mountains — they remove them. When a vast reservoir of silica-rich magma evacuates rapidly, the roof above it founders into the emptied chamber, collapsing the surface into a broad **caldera** that can be tens of kilometers across. The term **supereruption** is reserved for events that eject more than about **1,000 cubic kilometers** of magma, corresponding to the top of the **Volcanic Explosivity Index** at **VEI 8** (the **VEI 7-8** range covers the great caldera events). On the magnitude scale $M = \log_{10}(m) - 7$, where $m$ is the erupted mass in kilograms, supereruptions reach $M \gtrsim 8$.

The **Yellowstone** hotspot in the western United States is the archetype. It has produced at least three caldera-forming supereruptions: the **Huckleberry Ridge Tuff** about **2.1 million years ago** (~2,500 km3), the **Mesa Falls Tuff** about 1.3 Ma, and the **Lava Creek Tuff** about **640,000 years ago** (~1,000 km3), each blanketing much of North America in ash. Yellowstone's silicic system is fed by a continental hotspot, exactly the heat-induced crustal melting discussed earlier in this path. The **Long Valley Caldera** in California (the **Bishop Tuff**, ~760 ka) and the **Valles Caldera** in New Mexico are related North American examples.

The largest known eruption of the last hundred thousand years was **Toba** in Sumatra, Indonesia, about **74,000 years ago**, which expelled roughly **2,800 km3** of magma as the **Youngest Toba Tuff** and left a caldera ~100 km long now occupied by **Lake Toba**. The controversial **Toba catastrophe hypothesis** of **Stanley Ambrose** proposed that the eruption's climatic aftermath caused a human population bottleneck, though the severity and human impact remain debated. Even larger eruptions are preserved deep in the rock record, such as the **Fish Canyon Tuff** of the **La Garita Caldera** in Colorado (~28 Ma, ~5,000 km3), among the largest single eruptions ever identified, and the colossal **Oruanui** eruption of **Taupo** in New Zealand ~26,500 years ago.

A crucial point of perspective: supereruptions are **rare** — globally on the order of once every tens of thousands of years for VEI 8 — and none has occurred in recorded human history. The largest **historical** eruptions reached only **VEI 7**, an order of magnitude smaller in volume, yet even those, as the next slide shows, were enough to disrupt the global climate and human society profoundly. The gap between what humanity has witnessed and what the geologic record proves possible is one of the most sobering facts in the Earth sciences.

question.question: Why do the very largest explosive eruptions produce broad calderas rather than tall volcanic cones?
options: The magma is so hot it melts the mountain away
Rapid evacuation of a huge silicic magma reservoir removes support, so the overlying roof collapses into the emptied chamber, forming a broad depression
Erosion by ash removes the cone within hours
Calderas form only at mid-ocean ridges, never on land
question.explanation: A supereruption rapidly empties an enormous reservoir of viscous silicic magma. With its support withdrawn, the rock roof above founders downward into the void, collapsing the surface into a caldera tens of kilometers wide (as at Yellowstone and Toba). The volume erupted is too large and the withdrawal too rapid to build a cone; the ground subsides instead.

hints: What happens to the roof when a huge magma chamber empties quickly?
slides.workedSolution: When a vast silicic chamber erupts rapidly, the magma that supported the overlying crust is gone; the roof collapses into the emptied reservoir, producing a broad caldera rather than a cone. Yellowstone and Toba are the type examples. Option B is correct.

slides.title: Tambora and the Year Without a Summer
slides.body:
The most powerful eruption in recorded history is **Mount Tambora** on the island of **Sumbawa**, Indonesia, which erupted catastrophically in **April 1815** at **VEI 7**, ejecting on the order of **150-180 km3** of material and decapitating the mountain from roughly 4,300 m to 2,850 m. The immediate toll on Sumbawa and the surrounding region — from pyroclastic flows, tsunamis, ashfall, and the ensuing famine and disease — is estimated in the tens of thousands directly and perhaps 100,000 or more in total, making it among the deadliest eruptions ever.

But Tambora's most far-reaching legacy was atmospheric. The eruption injected an enormous mass of **sulfur dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$)** into the **stratosphere**, where it converted to a global veil of **sulfate aerosol** that reflected sunlight back to space for over a year. The result was the **1816 'Year Without a Summer'** (also called *eighteen-hundred-and-froze-to-death*). Across the Northern Hemisphere, average temperatures fell by roughly **0.4-0.7 °C** globally and considerably more regionally. **New England** and eastern Canada saw snow in June and killing frosts every month of the summer of 1816; crops failed repeatedly. **Western Europe** suffered a cold, sodden summer, ruined harvests, soaring grain prices, food riots, and one of the last great subsistence crises of the Western world.

The cultural and scientific consequences rippled outward in striking ways:
- The gloom of the wet summer kept **Mary Shelley**, **Lord Byron**, and **Percy Shelley** indoors at the Villa Diodati on **Lake Geneva**, where a ghost-story contest produced **Frankenstein** and **John Polidori's** *The Vampyre*.
- Crop failures and the death of horses for want of oats are credited with spurring **Karl Drais** to invent the **Laufmaschine** (the draisine, a precursor of the bicycle) in 1817.
- The vivid, sulfate-reddened sunsets of the period are thought to color the skies in paintings by **J. M. W. Turner**.
- Failed harvests pushed waves of migration and helped trigger the last major famine in the Western world (the Irish and broader European hardship of 1816-1817).

Tambora is therefore the clearest demonstration that a single eruption can perturb the entire climate system and reshape human history through a purely atmospheric mechanism. It also gives a calibration point: a VEI 7 eruption that loaded the stratosphere with sulfur cooled the planet by a fraction of a degree for a year or two. The next slide develops the physics of why sulfur, not ash, is the agent of that cooling, and how the magnitude of the forcing is estimated.

question.question: The 1815 Tambora eruption is classified at the VEI level just below the supereruption threshold. Given the VEI scale runs 0-8 and supereruptions are VEI 8, what VEI is Tambora? Answer with the number.
question.hint: It is the largest historical eruption, one step below VEI 8.

slides.title: Sulfate aerosols and radiative forcing
slides.body:
Why does a volcano cool the climate, and why is **sulfur**, not ash, the culprit? The answer lies in **stratospheric aerosols** and the planet's **radiative balance**.

Volcanic **ash** is heavy and settles out of the atmosphere within days to weeks; it has little lasting climatic effect. **Sulfur dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$)**, however, is a gas, and when a powerful eruption injects it above the tropopause into the dry, stable **stratosphere**, it oxidizes over weeks to **sulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$)** and condenses into a fine haze of micron-scale **sulfate aerosol** droplets:

$$ \text{SO}_2 + \text{OH} \rightarrow \dots \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \xrightarrow{\ \text{condensation}\ } \text{sulfate aerosol} $$

These droplets are nearly the right size to **scatter incoming sunlight** efficiently back to space while being too small and too high to settle quickly, so they linger for **1-3 years**, spread globally on stratospheric winds, and dim the surface. (They simultaneously absorb some radiation and warm the stratosphere itself, a diagnostic fingerprint of volcanic, as opposed to solar, forcing.)

The climatic effect is quantified as a **radiative forcing** $\Delta F$ — the change in net energy flux at the top of the atmosphere, in W/m2. The resulting equilibrium temperature change is $\Delta T = \lambda\,\Delta F$, where $\lambda$ is the **climate sensitivity** parameter. Volcanic forcing is negative (cooling) and scales with the **stratospheric sulfate mass**, often parameterized via aerosol **optical depth** $\tau$ as approximately $\Delta F \approx -21\,\tau$ W/m2 for large eruptions. The relevant facts:
- **Tambora (1815)** loaded the stratosphere with tens of teragrams of sulfur, drove a peak negative forcing of several W/m2, and cooled global mean surface temperature by ~0.4-0.7 °C — the Year Without a Summer.
- **Krakatoa (1883)** and especially **Mount Pinatubo (1991)** are the best-observed cases. Pinatubo injected ~17-20 Tg of $\text{SO}_2$, raised global stratospheric optical depth, and cooled the planet by about **0.5 °C** in 1992, a prediction that **James Hansen** and colleagues at **NASA GISS** made in advance using a climate model — a landmark validation of climate physics.
- The relationship $\Delta T \propto$ sulfur mass, not eruption volume, is why some large but sulfur-poor eruptions barely cool the climate while smaller sulfur-rich ones cool it markedly. **Mass of stratospheric sulfur is the master variable.**

The record extends deep into the past. The eruption of **Laki** in **Iceland** in **1783-84** released a colossal flux of $\text{SO}_2$ from a fissure (a high-latitude, low-VEI but high-sulfur event), causing a toxic 'dry fog' over Europe documented by **Benjamin Franklin** and a deadly cold spell. Ice cores from **Greenland** and **Antarctica** preserve sulfate spikes that let scientists reconstruct a multi-millennium history of volcanic forcing, and tree-ring records of cold summers corroborate them. The most extreme volcanic-climate hypotheses tie giant eruptions and the related **flood basalt** provinces (the **Deccan Traps**, the **Siberian Traps**) to mass extinctions. The unifying principle is clean and quantitative: explosive volcanism cools the climate in proportion to the **sulfate aerosol mass it places in the stratosphere**, through a measurable change in the planet's radiative balance.

question.question: Two eruptions have the same VEI and erupt similar volumes, but one cools global climate noticeably for two years while the other has almost no climatic effect. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The cooling eruption produced more ash, which blocked sunlight for years
The cooling eruption injected far more sulfur (SO2) into the stratosphere, forming long-lived sulfate aerosols, whereas the other was sulfur-poor
The cooling eruption happened in winter
Volume always determines climate impact, so the observation must be an error
question.explanation: Climatic cooling scales with the mass of sulfur delivered to the stratosphere, not with eruption volume or ash. Sulfur forms long-lived sulfate aerosols that scatter sunlight for 1-3 years. A sulfur-rich eruption (like Pinatubo or Tambora) cools the planet, while an equally large but sulfur-poor eruption does not. Ash settles out within weeks and contributes little to lasting forcing.

hints: Ash settles in weeks; what lingers for years?
The master variable is stratospheric sulfur mass, not volume.
slides.workedSolution: Lasting volcanic cooling comes from stratospheric sulfate aerosols, whose mass depends on how much SO2 the eruption injected, not on its bulk volume or ash. The sulfur-rich eruption forms a reflective, long-lived aerosol veil and cools the climate; the sulfur-poor one does not. Ash settles too quickly to matter. Option B is correct.

question.question: Anticipating the climate impact of a new eruption
question.prompt: A VEI 6 eruption in the tropics sends a strong, sulfur-rich plume well into the stratosphere, and satellite SO2 sensors estimate an injection comparable to Pinatubo in 1991. A colleague predicts catastrophic multi-year global cooling of several degrees. Using the physics of sulfate aerosols, radiative forcing, and the historical calibration from Pinatubo and Tambora, evaluate whether your colleague's estimate is reasonable, state the rough magnitude and duration of cooling you would actually expect, and explain why the eruption's tropical, high-altitude, sulfur-rich character matters.

slides.title: When volcanoes touch the whole planet
slides.body:
This lesson moved from the largest eruptions in the rock record to the physics by which volcanism reaches every corner of the globe.

**Supereruptions** evacuate more than ~1,000 km3 of silicic magma and collapse the ground into **calderas**. **Yellowstone** (the **Lava Creek**, **Mesa Falls**, and **Huckleberry Ridge** tuffs), **Toba** (~74 ka, the **Youngest Toba Tuff**, **Lake Toba**), **Long Valley** (**Bishop Tuff**), **Taupo** (**Oruanui**), and the immense **La Garita** (**Fish Canyon Tuff**) define the **VEI 7-8** range. They recur only every tens of thousands of years, and none has happened in recorded history.

**Tambora (1815)**, at VEI 7, is the largest historical eruption and the bridge to climate. Its stratospheric sulfur produced the **1816 Year Without a Summer**, with frosts in June across **New England**, harvest failures across **Europe**, the writing of **Frankenstein** at the Villa Diodati, and the invention of the **draisine**. It proves that even a sub-supereruption can perturb the global climate and human history.

The mechanism is **sulfate-aerosol radiative forcing**. Ash settles in weeks and barely matters; **$\text{SO}_2$** injected into the **stratosphere** becomes long-lived **sulfuric-acid aerosol** that scatters sunlight for 1-3 years. Cooling scales as $\Delta T = \lambda\,\Delta F$ with the **sulfur mass**, not the eruption volume — the lesson of **Pinatubo (1991)**, whose ~0.5 °C cooling **James Hansen** predicted in advance, and of high-sulfur **Laki (1783)**, recorded by **Benjamin Franklin** and in **Greenland** ice cores.

Three principles endure. **Volume builds calderas, but sulfur drives climate** — the two are decoupled. **The geologic record dwarfs human experience** — VEI 8 is real but unwitnessed. And **the physics is quantitative and predictive** — radiative forcing converts a sulfur mass into a temperature change with skill demonstrated by the Pinatubo forecast. With the science of eruptions, hazards, monitoring, and global impacts now complete, the final lesson looks forward: to the **satellite remote sensing**, **machine-learning forecasting**, **drones**, **geothermal energy**, and **planetary volcanism** that are carrying volcanology into its next era.
